triage.name: Ophthalmia neonatorum
triage.reason: Neonatal eye discharge with a clear differential by timing and organism; reachable via history, exam and conjunctival cultures.

demographics: Occurs in newborns; no sex predilection
More common where prenatal care is limited or maternal sexually transmitted infections are untreated

risk_factors.text: Maternal history of sexually transmitted infection

social_history: Mother may have untreated genital infection
exposures: Passage through an infected birth canal

chief_complaints.text: My baby's eye is red and swollen
There is pus coming from my baby's eye
My baby's eyelids are stuck together in the morning
My baby keeps the eye closed and seems uncomfortable

hpi.onset: Gradual, starting a few days after birth; gonococcal disease often appears at 2–5 days and chlamydial disease at 5–14 days
hpi.duration: Hours to days; present since the first week of life
hpi.progression: Discharge increases from watery to thick and purulent; eyelid swelling worsens; the eye may become difficult to open
hpi.location: One or both eyes, typically starting in one eye
hpi.quality: Thick yellow-green discharge with red, swollen conjunctiva and puffy eyelids
hpi.severity: Mild to moderate in most cases; severe with marked lid swelling and copious pus in gonococcal infection
hpi.timing: Continuous, worse after sleep when discharge dries and sticks the lids together

associated_symptoms.text: Redness of the white of the eye

pertinent_negatives: No watery eye discharge that is clear and non-purulent
No symptoms starting after 4 weeks of life
No known maternal sexually transmitted infection
No eye trauma or foreign body
No family history of glaucoma or retinoblastoma

atypical.how_it_differs: Preterm or low-birth-weight infants may have subtle signs such as mild redness without copious discharge, and systemic signs may be absent.
Neonates with immunodeficiency may have a more indolent or severe course with atypical organisms.

general.mild: Alert, feeding well, comfortable; one eye with mild redness and watery-to-mucoid discharge
general.moderate: Irritable but consolable, feeding adequately; eyelid swelling with thick discharge and lids stuck together after sleep
general.severe: Ill-appearing and fussy, feeding poorly; marked eyelid edema with copious purulent discharge, eye difficult to open
general.critical: Toxic-appearing, lethargic or inconsolable, poor feeding; tense swollen lids with profuse pus and possible corneal involvement

findings.maneuver: Inspect the conjunctiva of both eyes in good light
findings.finding: Diffuse conjunctival redness, worse in one eye

findings.maneuver: Inspect the palpebral fissure and lower fornix for discharge
findings.finding: Purulent yellow-green discharge pooling at the lid margin

findings.maneuver: Inspect and gently palpate the eyelids
findings.finding: Puffy, swollen eyelids that may be stuck together

findings.maneuver: Inspect the cornea with a penlight after gently parting the lids
findings.finding: Clear cornea without opacity or ulceration

findings.maneuver: Shine a direct ophthalmoscope light into each eye
Shine a light into each eye and observe the pupil response
Observe the infant tracking a light or face in all directions
findings.finding: Full, conjugate eye movements without restriction

findings.maneuver: Press gently over the medial canthus and lacrimal sac
findings.finding: No tenderness or expressible mucoid reflux from the punctum

findings.maneuver: Palpate the preauricular and submandibular lymph nodes

findings.finding: Normal tone and activity for age without focal deficit

labs.caveat: Neonatal white counts are normally higher than in older children; a normal count does not exclude gonococcal ophthalmia, and marked leukocytosis should raise concern for systemic infection.
Nonspecific; a rise supports invasive or systemic infection but does not identify the organism.
Can be elevated in the first days of life for noninfectious reasons; interpret with the clinical picture.

imaging.preferred_when: When the cornea or posterior segment cannot be seen because of lid swelling or discharge

initial.test: Conjunctival swab for Gram stain and culture
initial.why: Identifies Neisseria gonorrhoeae and guides therapy; Gram stain shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci

initial.test: Conjunctival swab for chlamydial nucleic acid amplification testing
initial.why: Detects Chlamydia trachomatis, the other major cause of neonatal conjunctivitis
Baseline white count and differential; helps assess for systemic illness
Baseline electrolytes and renal function before systemic antibiotics

initial.test: Maternal endocervical swab for gonorrhea and chlamydia
initial.why: Confirms the source of infection and guides treatment of the mother and partner

supporting.why: Supports concern for invasive or systemic infection when elevated
May support a systemic bacterial process when the infant appears ill
supporting.only_if: the infant appears systemically unwell or sepsis is suspected

supporting.why: Detects bacteremia in infants with suspected systemic gonococcal or other bacterial infection
supporting.only_if: the infant is ill-appearing, febrile, or has signs of systemic infection

supporting.why: Evaluates for pneumonia in an infant with respiratory signs or systemic illness
supporting.only_if: respiratory distress or systemic infection is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not routine for isolated conjunctivitis without respiratory or systemic signs
Not routine for a well-appearing infant with isolated conjunctivitis
Not needed when the eye can be examined directly
Lumbar puncture is not indicated for isolated conjunctivitis without meningeal or systemic signs

decision_points: Any newborn with purulent eye discharge in the first month of life needs conjunctival cultures and prompt treatment; do not wait for results in suspected gonococcal disease
Gonococcal ophthalmia is an ophthalmologic emergency because of the risk of corneal ulceration and perforation; admit and treat with systemic antibiotics
Chlamydial ophthalmia requires systemic therapy because topical treatment does not eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage and does not prevent pneumonia
Evaluate and treat the mother and her partner for gonorrhea and chlamydia
Consider other causes (chemical, nasolacrimal duct obstruction, herpes simplex) when cultures are negative and the course is atypical

differential.name: Chlamydial conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: The most common infectious cause of neonatal conjunctivitis; presents with purulent eye discharge in the first weeks of life
differential.trigger: Purulent eye discharge starting 5–14 days after birth in a vaginally delivered infant

history: Discharge starts watery and becomes mucopurulent
Mother may have untreated chlamydial infection or no prenatal care
exam: Eyelid swelling and conjunctival redness that may be milder than gonococcal disease
labs: Conjunctival nucleic acid amplification test positive for Chlamydia trachomatis
Gram stain shows no gram-negative intracellular diplococci
Giemsa stain may show intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies

differential.name: Gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum
differential.why_considered: The most severe cause of neonatal conjunctivitis; can rapidly progress to corneal ulceration and perforation
differential.trigger: Copious purulent discharge with marked eyelid swelling starting 2–5 days after birth

history: Mother may have untreated gonorrhea or no prenatal care
exam: Marked eyelid edema with copious yellow-green pus
Corneal haze or ulceration if advanced
labs: Gram stain shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci
Nucleic acid amplification test positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae

differential.name: Chemical conjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Noninfectious irritation from ocular prophylaxis at birth; presents with eye redness and watery discharge in the first days of life

history: Recent application of silver nitrate or other ocular prophylaxis
exam: Mild conjunctival redness without marked eyelid swelling

differential.name: Nasolacrimal duct obstruction
differential.why_considered: Common cause of watery eye and discharge in infants; can mimic infectious conjunctivitis

history: Chronic tearing and mucoid discharge since birth or early weeks
exam: Tearing with a normal or mildly red conjunctiva
Mucoid reflux expressible from the lacrimal sac on medial canthal pressure
labs: Cultures typically negative or grow normal flora

differential.name: Herpes simplex virus keratoconjunctivitis
differential.why_considered: Neonatal HSV can present with conjunctivitis and eye discharge; sight-threatening and systemically dangerous
differential.trigger: Vesicles on the skin or eyelids, or a mother with active genital herpes at delivery

history: May have skin vesicles or systemic signs
exam: Vesicles on the eyelids, face, or skin
Dendritic corneal lesions on fluorescein staining
labs: HSV polymerase chain reaction positive from conjunctival swab

differential.name: Congenital glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Presents with red, watery eyes and photophobia in infants; can be mistaken for conjunctivitis
differential.trigger: Corneal clouding, photophobia, or an enlarged eye in an infant with watery eyes

history: Progressive eye enlargement noted by parents
imaging: Ocular ultrasound may show increased axial length

severity.mild: Mild redness and watery-to-mucoid discharge in one eye; infant feeding well and comfortable
severity.moderate: Thick purulent discharge with eyelid swelling and lids stuck together after sleep; infant irritable but consolable
severity.severe: Marked eyelid edema with copious purulent discharge, eye difficult to open; infant fussy and feeding poorly
severity.critical: Corneal ulceration or perforation, or systemic infection with sepsis; infant toxic-appearing, lethargic, or inconsolable

red_flags.meaning: Ophthalmologic emergency; risk of permanent vision loss, especially with gonococcal infection

red_flags.finding: Marked eyelid edema with copious purulent discharge
red_flags.meaning: Suggests gonococcal ophthalmia; requires prompt systemic antibiotics and admission
Possible systemic infection or sepsis; needs urgent evaluation and cultures
Suggests neonatal herpes simplex virus; requires systemic antiviral therapy
Suggests congenital glaucoma; urgent ophthalmology referral

complications.name: Corneal perforation and vision loss
clues: Sudden eye pain and decreased vision
Copious purulent discharge with marked lid swelling

complications.name: Chlamydial pneumonia
clues: Cough and tachypnea weeks after conjunctivitis

special_populations.differences: Preterm or low-birth-weight infants may have subtle signs such as mild redness without copious discharge; systemic signs may be absent.
Neonates with immunodeficiency may have a more indolent or severe course with atypical organisms.

key_questions.question: How old was your baby when the eye symptoms started?
key_questions.looking_for: Timing narrows the cause: chemical (first 24-48 hours), gonococcal (2-5 days), chlamydial (5-14 days)

key_questions.question: What does the discharge look like - watery, or thick and pus-like?
key_questions.looking_for: Copious thick yellow-green pus suggests gonococcal disease; watery or mucoid suggests chemical or nasolacrimal duct obstruction

key_questions.question: Is one eye or both eyes affected?
key_questions.looking_for: Often starts in one eye but can become bilateral; both eyes from birth suggests chemical or obstruction

key_questions.question: Is the eyelid swollen, and is the eye hard to open?
key_questions.looking_for: Marked eyelid edema with copious pus suggests gonococcal ophthalmia

key_questions.question: Is the baby feeding well and acting normally, or is he/she fussy, sleepy, or feeding poorly?
key_questions.looking_for: Fever, lethargy, or poor feeding suggests systemic infection or sepsis

key_questions.question: Did the baby receive eye drops or ointment at birth?
key_questions.looking_for: Ocular prophylaxis can cause chemical conjunctivitis within 24-48 hours

key_questions.question: Was the baby born vaginally or by cesarean section?
key_questions.looking_for: Vaginal delivery through an infected birth canal is the usual route of infection

key_questions.question: How long were your membranes ruptured before delivery?
key_questions.looking_for: Prolonged rupture increases risk of infection

key_questions.question: Did you have any prenatal care? Were you tested or treated for gonorrhea or chlamydia during pregnancy?
key_questions.looking_for: Untreated maternal gonorrhea or chlamydia is the key risk factor

key_questions.question: Have you had any genital discharge, sores, or burning with urination?
key_questions.looking_for: Symptoms of maternal sexually transmitted infection

key_questions.question: Do you have a history of genital herpes?
key_questions.looking_for: Maternal HSV raises concern for neonatal herpes keratoconjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Any skin blisters or vesicles on the baby?
key_questions.looking_for: Vesicles suggest neonatal herpes simplex virus

key_questions.question: Any cough, trouble breathing, or noisy breathing?
key_questions.looking_for: Chlamydial pneumonia can follow or accompany conjunctivitis

key_questions.question: Any eye trauma, foreign body, or exposure to irritants?
key_questions.looking_for: Alternative cause of eye redness and discharge

reasoning_points: Age at onset is the key clue: chemical within 24-48 hours, gonococcal at 2-5 days, chlamydial at 5-14 days
Character of discharge: copious thick purulent discharge suggests gonococcal disease; watery or mucoid suggests chemical or nasolacrimal duct obstruction
Maternal history of untreated gonorrhea or chlamydia, or lack of prenatal care, supports an infectious cause
Vaginal delivery through an infected birth canal is the usual mechanism
Marked eyelid edema with copious pus and possible corneal involvement indicates gonococcal ophthalmia, an emergency
Conjunctival swabs for Gram stain, culture, and chlamydial nucleic acid amplification testing identify the organism
Gonococcal disease requires systemic antibiotics and admission because of the risk of corneal ulceration and perforation
Chlamydial disease requires systemic therapy because topical treatment does not eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage or prevent pneumonia
The mother and her partner must be evaluated and treated for gonorrhea and chlamydia
Consider herpes simplex virus when vesicles are present or the mother has genital herpes, and congenital glaucoma when the cornea is cloudy or the eye is enlarged

easy: Vaginally delivered newborn with copious purulent eye discharge at 3 days of life
Mother with no prenatal care and known untreated gonorrhea
Marked eyelid swelling with thick yellow-green pus and eye difficult to open
Gram stain shows gram-negative intracellular diplococci
medium: Newborn with watery-to-mucoid discharge and mild redness in the first 48 hours after ocular prophylaxis
Infant with purulent discharge at 7-10 days and a mother with untreated chlamydia
Chronic tearing and mucoid discharge since birth with a normal conjunctiva
Bilateral eye discharge in a well-appearing infant with no maternal risk factors
hard: Preterm infant with subtle redness and little discharge
Infant with vesicles on the eyelids and a mother with genital herpes
Infant with corneal clouding and an enlarged globe mistaken for conjunctivitis
Ill-appearing infant with fever, poor feeding, and eye discharge suggesting systemic infection
Negative conjunctival cultures with an atypical or persistent course
